--- title: "Graph Theory: Blockmodeling" subtitle: "Role Structure and Block Relations" format: revealjs: scrollable: true theme: default css: ucla-theme.css width: 1280 height: 720 margin: 0.1 min-scale: 0.2 --- # Part 1: The Correlation Distance & CONCOR --- ## The Correlation Distance ($d^{corr}_{k,l}$) ::: {.incremental} - Beyond Euclidean distance, we can measure structural similarity using the **Pearson Correlation Coefficient** ($r_{kl}$ or $d^{corr}_{kl}$) between node vectors. - Compares row (or column) vectors and returns a value between **$-1.0$ and $+1.0$**: - **$+1.0$**: Nodes are perfectly structurally equivalent. - **Positive ($> 0.0$)**: Nodes are structurally similar. - **Negative ($< 0.0$)**: Nodes are structurally dissimilar. - **$-1.0$**: Nodes are completely different, pointing to completely disjoint sets of neighbors. - The formula is: - $$d^{corr}_{k, l} = \frac{\sum_j (a_{(k)j} - \overline{a}_{(k)j}) \times (a_{(l)j} - \overline{a}_{(l)j})}{\sqrt{\sum_j (a_{(k)j} - \overline{a}_{(k)j})^2 \times \sum_j (a_{(l)j} - \overline{a}_{(l)j})^2}}$$ ::: --- ## Meaning of Row Means ($\overline{a}_{(k)j}$) ::: {.incremental} - What does $\overline{a}_{(k)j}$ represent? - It is simply the **average of the row elements** for node $k$. - $$\overline{a}_{(k)j} = \frac{\sum_j a_{kj}}{N}$$ - Where $N$ is the number of columns (the order of the graph). - For a binary adjacency matrix, the row mean is simply the **node degree divided by the number of nodes**: - Node $A$ has ties to $\{C, D\}$ in a 6-node network: - Vector $a_{(A)j} = (0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0)$. - Average: $\overline{a}_{(A)j} = \frac{2}{6} \approx 0.33$. ::: --- ## Mean Differences Vector - Subtracting the row mean $\overline{a}_{(A)j} \approx 0.33$ from each entry of $A$'s row vector $a_{(A)j} = (0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0)$ gives the Mean Differences vector: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
A B C D E F
Row A 0 0 1 1 0 0
A - Mean (0 - 0.33) (0 - 0.33) (1 - 0.33) (1 - 0.33) (0 - 0.33) (0 - 0.33)
Difference -0.33 -0.33 0.67 0.67 -0.33 -0.33
````` ::: ::: - We compute these difference vectors for all pairs of nodes, multiply them in the numerator, normalize them in the denominator, and obtain the correlation matrix. --- ## Correlation Distance Matrix ($S^{corr}$) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
A B C D E F
A -- 1 -0.71 -0.5 0.25 -0.32
B 1 -- -0.71 -0.5 0.25 -0.32
C -0.71 -0.71 -- 0.71 -0.71 0.45
D -0.5 -0.5 0.71 -- -0.5 -0.32
E 0.25 0.25 -0.71 -0.5 -- -0.32
F -0.32 -0.32 0.45 -0.32 -0.32 --
````` ::: ::: - Structurally equivalent pairs ($\{A, B\}$ and $\{C, D\}$) have a correlation of **1.00**. - Completely disjoint pairs ($\{C, E\}$ and $\{D, E\}$) are perfectly negatively correlated (**-1.00**). - Similar but non-equivalent nodes ($C$ and $F$) have a correlation of **0.45**. --- ## Iterated Correlation Distances: CONCOR ::: {.incremental} - What happens if we take the correlation distance of a correlation distance matrix? - **CONCOR** (Convergence of Iterated Correlations; Breiger, Boorman, & Arabie, 1975): - If we recursively calculate the correlation distance matrix of the previous correlation matrix, the values mathematically **converge to only $+1.0$ and $-1.0$**. - This slices the network into two distinct, highly clear-cut blocks of structurally equivalent or similar nodes. - Let's look at this mathematical convergence in action. ::: --- ## Iterative Convergence (2nd & 3rd Iterations) :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ### 2nd Iteration Matrix - Values begin polarizing toward $+1$ and $-1$. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
A B C D E F
A -- 1 -0.93 -0.78 0.68 -0.57
B 1 -- -0.93 -0.78 0.68 -0.57
C -0.93 -0.93 -- 0.85 -0.9 0.6
D -0.78 -0.78 0.85 -- -0.76 0.08
E 0.68 0.68 -0.9 -0.76 -- -0.54
F -0.57 -0.57 0.6 0.08 -0.54 --
````` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ### 3rd Iteration Matrix - Every cell reaches **exactly $+1.00$ or $-1.00$**! ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
A B C D E F
A -- 1 -0.99 -0.95 0.96 -0.86
B 1 -- -0.99 -0.95 0.96 -0.86
C -0.99 -0.99 -- 0.96 -0.99 0.86
D -0.95 -0.95 0.96 -- -0.95 0.69
E 0.96 0.96 -0.99 -0.95 -- -0.85
F -0.86 -0.86 0.86 0.69 -0.85 --
````` ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Structural Positions via CONCOR ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
A B C D E F
A 1.00 1.00 -0.99 -0.95 0.96 -0.86
B 1.00 1.00 -0.99 -0.95 0.96 -0.86
C -0.99 -0.99 1.00 0.96 -0.99 0.86
D -0.95 -0.95 0.96 1.00 -0.95 0.69
E 0.96 0.96 -0.99 -0.95 1.00 -0.85
F -0.86 -0.86 0.86 0.69 -0.85 1.00
````` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - By analyzing the rows of $+1$ and $-1$, we extract perfect structurally equivalent positions: - Position 1 (Salmon): Nodes $\{A, B\}$ - Position 2 (Green): Nodes $\{C, D\}$ - Position 3 (Blue): Node $\{E\}$ - Position 4 (Purple): Node $\{F\}$ ::: # Part 2: Blockmodeling a 22-Node Network --- ## Uncovering Secret Patterns in Large Networks :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - Let's apply CONCOR to a larger, messier 22-node network on the right. - It contains: - Three high-degree hub nodes ($A$, $B$, $C$). - Sets of identical peripheral leaf nodes connected to each hub. - A highly central node $D$ bridging hubs. - Two peripheral nodes $U, V$ connected only to $S$. - Let's see how CONCOR recursively partitions this graph. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](blockmodeling_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Step 1: First Split (Two Giant Blocks) - Running CONCOR on the whole 22-node network splits it into two massive blocks: - **Block 1**: $\{V, U, S, H, G, F, E, T, C, A, B\}$ (Colored Red) - **Block 2**: $\{R, Q, P, O, N, M, L, K, J, D, I\}$ (Colored Blue) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](blockmodeling_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: --- ## Step 2: Going Deeper (The Hierarchical Partition) ::: {.incremental} - Running CONCOR recursively on the induced subgraphs of each block yields nested subdivisions: - **Block 1 Splits**: - **Block 1a** (Core hub/bridge): $\{A, B, C, S, U, V\}$ - **Block 1b** (A's peripheral leaves): $\{E, F, G, H, T\}$ - **Block 2 Splits**: - **Block 2a** (B's peripheral leaves): $\{I, J, K, L, M\}$ - **Block 2b** (C's peripheral leaves): $\{N, O, P, Q, R\}$ - **Block 2c** (Unique central bridge): $\{D\}$ (Occupies a block entirely by itself!) - Further splits on Block 1a isolate $\{U, V\}$, and divide the remaining $\{A, B, C, S\}$ into $\{A, S\}$ and $\{B, C\}$. ::: --- ## Final Seven-Block Partition - The final, elegant block partition reveals how role structures are naturally isolated: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](blockmodeling_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: --- ## The Blocked Adjacency Matrix ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - **Thick black lines** divide the matrix into block submatrices. - Diagonal squares represent **within-block** ties; off-diagonal rectangles represent **between-block** ties. - We identify **Zero Blocks** (filled only with 0s) and **One Blocks** (containing some 1s). ::: # Part 3: Image Matrices & Reduced Graphs --- ## Reducing Complexity to an Image Matrix ::: {.incremental} - The blocked adjacency matrix can be simplified to a **reduced image matrix** ($\mathbf{B}$) of dimensions $b \times b$ (where $b = 7$ is the number of blocks). - **Rule of Reduction**: - We record a **0** if the relation block is a **Zero Block** (completely disconnected). - We record a **1** if the relation block is a **One Block** (contains ties). - This yields a highly simplified map of role interactions: - $$ \mathbf{B} = \begin{pmatrix} \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} & \text{One} & \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} \\ \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} & \text{One} & \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} \\ \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} & \text{One} & \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} \\ \text{One} & \text{One} & \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} & \text{One} \\ \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} & \text{One} & \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} & \text{One} & \text{One} \\ \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} & \text{One} & \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} \\ \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} & \text{One} & \text{One} & \text{Zero} & \text{Zero} \end{pmatrix} $$ ::: --- ## Image Matrix Table ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Leaves_I Leaves_N Leaves_T Hubs_BC Hubs_AS Leaves_UV Bridge_D
Leaves_I 0 0 0 1 0 0 0
Leaves_N 0 0 0 1 0 0 0
Leaves_T 0 0 0 0 1 0 0
Hubs_BC 1 1 0 0 0 0 1
Hubs_AS 0 0 1 0 0 1 1
Leaves_UV 0 0 0 0 1 0 0
Bridge_D 0 0 0 1 1 0 0
````` ::: ::: - High-level representation of block relations. - Notice that Leaf blocks do not connect to themselves (0s on diagonal), but connect specifically to their respective Hub blocks. --- ## Reduced Graph Representation :::: {.columns align=center} ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.incremental} - We can plot the image matrix as a **reduced graph**. - **The Power of Blockmodeling**: - Distills a sprawling, complex network of 22 nodes down to a highly intuitive role-interaction model of just **7 block-nodes**. - Revealing the structural blueprint of the system: peripheral elements (leaves) feeding into coordinated brokers (hubs), bridged by a highly central node ($D$). ::: ::: ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](blockmodeling_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-align='center' width=624} ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Blockmodeling: A Structural Summary ::: {.incremental} - **Blockmodeling Distills Structure**: - Slices complex social structures down to high-level system blueprints. - **CONCOR algorithm**: - Recursively polarizes Pearson correlations to group similar actors. - **Zero vs. One Blocks**: - Blocked adjacency matrices cleanly isolate patterns of connection (One blocks) and absolute separation (Zero blocks). - **Reduced Graph Models**: - Image matrices represent relations *between roles*, creating simplified reduced graphs that make networks easy to read, interpret, and model. :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
